extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, media policymakers, and media critics interested in news reform and news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for organizing national news so it represents many perspectives (a two-tier system, balance over time, source access, monitoring, funding). Focuses on how to select, allocate space, fund, and monitor multiperspectival news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-tier media model
rubrics_metrics.description: Central (first-tier) media complemented by a second tier of pre-existing and new national media serving specific, fairly homogeneous audiences (daily/weekly/monthly TV, radio, newspapers, magazines). Second-tier outlets would primarily reanalyze and reinterpret news gathered by central media and wire services for their audiences, add commentary, and back these up with as much original reporting as financially feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-tier organizations will likely be small and may need subsidies. They supply bottom-up, representative, and service news; they can function as monitors and critics of central media by indicating where central media have been insufficiently multiperspectival. Examples: ethnic/racial press, journals of opinion, small-party publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central media should become more multiperspectival
rubrics_metrics.description: Central media must become more multiperspectival because they remain most prominent in the symbolic arena; the degree of multiperspectivism should be considered as an allocation of the scarce national 'newshole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no simple formulas; many judgments left to journalists. The key issue: how to allocate limited space/time among many sources and perspectives so journalism can accomplish its work and attract audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redefinition of newsworthiness / importance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should redefine importance considerations to give greater weight to information that is important to various sectors of the population, and less weight to 'nation' and 'society' as undifferentiated units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public officials (and corporate officials etc.) become newsworthy when their actions/statements significantly impact one or more major sectors/roles. Stories grow in importance with the number of affected sectors or with drastic impact on a few. Impact should be measured by output indicators. Social/moral disorder is important when it affects public/private policy or involves people who lack other means of appearing in the symbolic arena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiperspectival balance (priority to balance considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of multiperspectivism is greater balance: journalists must prioritize balance in news judgment and be knowledgeable about the universe of possible sources and perspectives to represent them in a balanced fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because perfect mapping may be impossible, the modest solution is to go beyond current practice to ensure more unrepresented sources appear. Balance should be achieved over time (e.g., running stories or over a year's time), not necessarily within a single story. Use demographic/sectoral representation as a target (example: if ~15% population is poor, aim for ~15% of coverage of income groups to deal with the poor). Exceptions: wartime, catastrophes, major public initiatives, or inherently newsworthy figures (presidents, criminals) may legitimately distort balance temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of beneficiaries, victims, and diverse political spokespeople
rubrics_metrics.description: For government or corporate activity coverage, prime additional sources for bottom-up and output news are beneficiaries and victims; for political news, include major and some minor parties, other groups likely affected, and representatives of positions across the ideological spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying beneficiaries/victims requires reporter legwork. Journalists should expand beyond the usual official and elite spokespeople to include those who will be affected by actions and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative and service news about marginalized groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Report more representative and service news about people currently omitted or poorly covered: the poor, blue-collar and lower white-collar workers, the old, children and adolescents, racial minorities, and those whose opinions conflict with various 'mainstreams.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these people, their problems, and their opinions as respectfully as those of high officials; avoid treating them only as public officials, spokespersons, deviants, or oddities. Feasible balance for very large universes is difficult; prioritize numerically and politically significant sectors and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping the universe of sources and perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieving multiperspectivalism requires (ideally) a complete 'mapping' of all sources and perspectives in society by social scientists, statisticians, and journalists; such mapping is not now available but is a desirable objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of full mapping, the modest approach is to ensure more of currently unrepresented sources are included. Mapping can guide story selection and balance assessments but responsibility for checking balance should belong to monitors and critics rather than press staff alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should select the news — regulated sharing of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of who allocates scarce news resources matters: journalists have insisted on sole responsibility, but the author argues journalists should share responsibility with others, provided sharing results in widespread and democratic participation rather than domination by advertisers or vocal interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any sharing must be regulated to avoid capture by advertisers, best-organized groups, or other vested interests. Professional self-regulation tends to favor professionals' own interests and government regulation risks co-optation of journalists; alternatives like boards or elected editors have practical problems (co-optation, packed electorates). Second-tier media might experiment with democratic organization and lay reporters/commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect sharing of responsibility via access, criticism, and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: If direct sharing is problematic, responsibility can be shared indirectly by: giving unrepresented sources greater access to journalists; strengthening external criticism of the news media; democratizing opportunities to exert pressure; and expanding audience feedback mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources need funds and media-savvy intermediaries to gain access. Encourage reasoned, constructive letters and organizational criticism; support lay reviewers and independent media criticism programs; recognize journalists may resent or ignore pressure yet must adapt to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-media criticism and monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish television and radio programs and independent publications to review the news; create commercial, academic, public-interest, and other agencies to monitor news content and evaluate balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring studies should be published in lay language and ideally funded/carried out by disinterested parties, though ideologically motivated analyses are acceptable if values are spelled out and analyses represent all parts of political/ideological spectrums. Monitors must themselves be balanced to avoid bias toward affluent/conservative agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience research as democratizing pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use audience research (random sampling) to reach people unwilling or unable to exert pressure; regular studies of how people attend to news, what they find useful/deficient, and what they want should be conducted and published to exert pressure on news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies must be published to be a form of pressure. Carry out audience research by both disinterested and interested agencies (each will ask different questions), ensuring interested agencies are balanced across ideological perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish legal pressure that restricts sources; protect sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectivism requires abolition of legal pressure that reduces journalists' access to sources (e.g., court decisions that restrict source protections), and protections for sources' anonymity to maximize incentives to provide information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal rulings that increase vulnerability of governmental adversaries or others discourage information supply; journalists should be able to shield sources from harm; source protection remains crucial even when lives may be at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize news as a public utility as well as a consumer product
rubrics_metrics.description: News should be regarded not solely as a consumer product but also as a utility inherently necessary for the proper functioning of democratic society; this status justifies public support even if audience growth is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiperspectival news supplies representation in the symbolic arena and feedback for public officials; treating news as a utility supports arguments for government funding (e.g., an Endowment for News) to correct inequities of commercial media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment grant program — Program 1: funds for entrepreneurs creating second-tier national media
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Endowment for News would provide funds to entrepreneurs, including journalists, interested in creating new, second-tier national media who can demonstrate intent to reach existing or currently unreached audiences with unavailable sources and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must demonstrate capacity to reach target audiences and add new perspectives; funds would target projects unable to obtain support elsewhere; the Endowment could supply/underwrite loans for initial capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment grant program — Program 2: aid to existing national news media to add perspectives and create new programs/sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Endowment would aid existing national news media prepared to add new sources and perspectives to the news and to establish new television/radio programs or magazine/newspaper sections for that purpose; also aid existing firms wanting to establish second-tier media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support is contingent on demonstrating that the proposed additions will increase multiperspectival coverage and that alternative funding is unavailable or insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment grant program — Program 3: support for sources to gain access to journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: The Endowment would support organized or unorganized sources who can demonstrate present inability to gain access to national journalists by supplying funds to establish facilitating mechanisms used by public agencies and others to obtain access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funds would help sources create media events, prepare spokespersons, or use media specialists to become accessible to national journalists; applicants must show inability to obtain funds elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment grant program — Program 4: support for criticism, monitoring, and pressure organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Endowment would help new and existing organizations, journalistic and other, engaged in criticism and monitoring of the news; it would also support organizations that seek to exert pressure on news media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding should encourage the creation of monitoring studies and public criticism in lay language; recipients may include commercial, academic, public-interest, or other agencies. The Endowment should support a diversity of ideological perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment grant program — Program 5: support for audience feedback mechanisms and news research
rubrics_metrics.description: The Endowment would support new and existing organizations in creating or improving audience feedback mechanisms and in conducting news research among present and potential audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants would fund mechanisms that broaden audience input (letters, research dissemination) and both disinterested and interested research, provided interested researchers disclose perspectives and balance is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment grant program — Program 6: direct assistance to individuals lacking access
rubrics_metrics.description: The Endowment would provide funds directly or indirectly to people too poor to obtain national newspapers and magazines or to afford television sets and radios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assistance could take various forms (subscriptions, device provision); recipients must demonstrate need; program aims to expand the potential audience for multiperspectival news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment governance, eligibility, and safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Endowment would not participate in news selection or production; its sole responsibility is provision of funds limited to applicants without other support. Applicants must demonstrate alternative funding is unavailable; grant recipients must find other sources for at least 25–33% of their budget to avoid total dependence. The Endowment would be run by an independent board (journalists and lay people) and use peer review committees that include journalists and nonjournalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review procedures modeled on federal agencies' peer review while ensuring inclusion of nonjournalists. For start-up capital, the Endowment might underwrite loans. Detailed guidelines required to assess whether applicants will add new perspectives. Matching funds requirement to reduce intimidation/co-optation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of limitations and risks of public funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Government funding of news entails risks: corruption and incompetence in granting agencies, political pressure on the Endowment not to fund unpopular ideas, potential for subtle pressures on recipients to favor incumbents, governmental review leading to regulation, and chilling effects if run directly from the White House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include independent governance, inclusion of journalists and nonjournalists on boards and committees, matching funds to avoid total dependence, peer review procedures, and transparency. The author judges these dangers not fatal but real and in need of safeguards.
